Meanwhile, the database cache quietly absorbs repeated read requests, sparing the primary store from constant pressure; every cache hit returns data in microseconds, while a miss forces a slower round trip to disk before the result reaches the application layer.

However, not every cache behaves the same way under real load; a write-through cache updates storage immediately, while a write-back cache waits and improves throughput, so raw speed can trade against durability. Engineers must weigh these trade-offs carefully, since a wrong policy can silently corrupt results or waste costly memory on data nobody requests again.

Along this path, a fast RAM layout can avoid a slow disk lookup, and it should not add risk or cost during a busy day. Traffic can jump up, but a hash lookup stays quick, and this stops any slow crawl toward a full disk scan.

Finally, teams should test thoroughly, monitor hit ratios, and tune eviction policies over time; the rollout can be marked done.
